name: Marco Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. What you say here is confidential. Walk me through a usual day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 27 and manage eleven fraud review analysts at a big payments company. I start with accounts that were frozen overnight, look for wrongful blocks, and decide which cases need an analyst to call a customer. I use AI every day to sort case notes and compare unusual patterns, but the team still signs the final decision. I like finding the one error that saves a small shop from losing a day of sales.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You seem young for that responsibility. What is home like, and how much room do you have if work changes?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I earned an MBA, then built a case review process that cut repeat mistakes, so they gave me the team. I’m single and rent a flat by myself; my pay is typical for a manager here, with about three months of expenses saved. There are some other large companies nearby, though few advertise posts every month. I’m comfortable trying tools early, and I’m also a member of the staff association because workers should see the terms of any change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the analysts that a tool can arrange case notes, but people still need to unfreeze a shop’s account when a rule gets it wrong. I’d share the small time savings instead of chasing another daily quota.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My role should remain, and three months saved makes me reasonably comfortable. I’d be disappointed that the better tools I imagined didn’t arrive, but disappointment isn’t a lost paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I’d keep using AI to sort the morning notes and keep the human sign-off on every account closure. During the first year I’d move 90 a month to savings and ask the staff association to review any new case targets before they start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the job and money. I might grumble about slow software, then go home and cook dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to a shop whose account is still frozen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would call the owner, explain what record we need, and give a time for the next answer. A sorted note is useless if the shop cannot take payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the association review in a quiet year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether saved minutes turn into a tougher target without more pay. My team should get a say even when the tool only saves a little time.

say: I’d keep **human sign-off** on frozen accounts.
Small time savings should not become a hidden **quota rise**.
I’d keep **case targets** open to staff review.
think: My **management job** looks secure because people still review frozen accounts.
Three months of **savings** give me room to pay rent through a short interruption.
do: Continue **morning note sorting** and human account sign-off.
Save **90 monthly** and ask the association to review case targets.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and money.
S0.quote: A sorted note is useless if the shop cannot take payment.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily** to organize fraud case notes.
The plateau preserves his **management role** and three-month reserve.
He watches for **quota changes** even when software saves little time.

steps.text: Keep sorting morning fraud notes with AI and require human account sign-off
Transfer 90 monthly into savings during the first year
Ask the staff association to review new fraud case targets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell my team the software will handle much of our checking and written replies, so we should test false freezes before rolling it out. I’d ask the staff association to press for paid training and a right to challenge bad decisions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can learn faster than many managers, but the company may merge review teams when routine checks disappear. Being good with the tool might win me a transition role; it could also make my present job smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d build a test set of 300 past wrongful freezes and compare AI flags with the case record. In the first year I’d take a paid company course in system audits and ask the association to negotiate a person on every appeal, while keeping my savings transfer if pay holds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about a merged team and the analysts who have only done basic reviews. I’m also curious to see whether we can reduce unfair freezes without hiding the errors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you trust to judge the test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask Priya, our most careful analyst, and a staff association representative to inspect the mistakes separately. Their disagreement would tell us where the tool is weak.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you be honest about a result showing six posts could go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, and I’d put that number in the association meeting before management makes an announcement. Fast software is no excuse for a secret staffing decision.

say: I’d test **wrongful freezes** before live use.
Staff need **paid training** and a person on each appeal.
Management should share **staffing effects** before the rollout.
think: A **team merger** could remove my current post.
My tool skills might help, but they do not **guarantee work**.
do: Test **300 old cases** for false flags this month.
Complete a **paid audit course** and negotiate human appeals through the association.
feel: I feel **anxious** and curious about the test.
S1.quote: Fast software is no excuse for a secret staffing decision.
fieldNote: He chooses **wrongful freezes** as the practical measure of tool quality.
He sees a possible **team merger** despite his technical skill.
He shares staffing evidence with the **association** before management acts.

steps.text: Test AI flags against 300 past wrongful account freezes
Complete a paid company course in system audits
Ask the staff association to negotiate a person on every account appeal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company to disclose when fraud review posts will close and who customers can reach after an AI freeze. I’d tell the staff association to bargain for paid retraining before a single team is dissolved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fraud review is thinking work from start to finish, so I expect my role to go when AGI arrives in 2028. Robots for hands-on jobs around 2031 give me a narrow window elsewhere, not a safe career; three months of rent money can run out quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomorrow I’d ask the association to demand a written severance and training agreement and cut my concert spending by 60 a month. Before 2028 I’d apply for a paid water-system maintenance apprenticeship and enroll if offered; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d stay in it only if the wage covers my rent and the employer guarantees supervised work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. I can make calls and learn, but two years is a small runway for changing trades while keeping my flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why water-system maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’ve spent weekends helping at a community repair workshop and want to learn the real trade under supervision. The hands-on part might need people until 2031, but I would not pretend robots stop there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the apprenticeship offer pays too little?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep applying for paid roles and use the severance terms if I lost my job. I wouldn’t sign for a trainee wage that leaves the rent unpaid.

say: I’d ask for **closure dates** and a customer contact after AI freezes.
The association should bargain for **paid retraining**.
think: My **fraud review job** could end in 2028.
Three months saved cannot fund a long **trade switch** alone.
do: Ask the **association** for written severance and training terms.
Cut **concert spending** by 60 monthly starting tomorrow.
Apply for a **paid water-system apprenticeship** and enroll only with rent-covering pay and supervision.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the short runway.
S2.quote: I wouldn’t sign for a trainee wage that leaves the rent unpaid.
fieldNote: His **thinking work** faces the 2028 deadline directly.
The maintenance route has a **2031 robot horizon**, which he recognizes.
He requires **supervision and rent-covering pay** before taking an apprenticeship.

steps.text: Join the staff association demand for written severance and paid training terms
Reduce concert spending by 60 monthly starting now
Enroll in a paid water-system apprenticeship if offered with rent-covering wages and supervised work
Apply for a paid water-system apprenticeship before 2028 with rent-covering wages and supervised work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to publish a staffing plan in stages and fund places for people who want another trade. I’d want the association at the table before the first team is merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could finish an apprenticeship before the thinking work vanishes in 2031 if a utility takes me and pays enough. The hands-on robots around 2034 make it a bridge, so I’d also learn how the machines are repaired rather than just follow a checklist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I’d enroll in a weekend electrical safety course if my company covers the fee, and I’d use two saved vacation days for supervised practice at the community repair workshop. I’d apply for posted utility technician apprenticeships before 2031 if the wage covers rent; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay in the paid program while learning machine servicing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but I can test my interest before leaving the fraud team. Five years makes a real application possible, assuming the vacancies exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much of your savings would you spend on that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company needs to cover the fee, so I’d spend only the two vacation days and travel fare. Three months of savings is for rent during a job change, not a stack of certificates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stay in fraud review instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A funded role handling disputed freezes with a clear person accountable might persuade me for a while. I’d still keep the technical applications moving, because that role may disappear by 2031.

The association should join before any **team merger**.
think: I could qualify before **2031 AGI** if a paid place opens.
The **2034 robots** could also change utility maintenance.
do: Enroll in **electrical safety** only if the fee is covered.
Use two **vacation days** for supervised practice and apply for viable apprenticeships.
feel: I feel **anxious** but can test a new route.
S3.quote: Three months of savings is for rent during a job change, not a stack of certificates.
fieldNote: He makes the course conditional on **company funding**.
He uses **supervised practice** to test actual hands-on work.
He keeps applications tied to **posted paid places**, mindful of rent.

Ask the staff association to join the staged staffing talks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d argue for publishing error rates and staff numbers each year, so workers and customers can judge the transition. The association could use ten years to win a fair share of the savings, not merely a final notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d like to build the appeal system well and then leave the fraud desk on my own terms. A decade would let me clear my loan and build a longer reserve, though I still expect the thinking parts of my job to be exposed in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d propose a yearly public count of wrongful freezes and ask the association to negotiate staff input before AI rules change. I’d pay an extra 140 a month toward my MBA loan while my income holds, then apply for a paid utility training post before 2036; in the first year after AGI, I’d remain in that post only while the wage covers rent and there is real supervised work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the end point, but less cornered. Ten years is long enough to repay the loan without betting everything on a new trade tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a public count instead of an internal one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small shop whose account is frozen should know whether mistakes are rising. I’d strip out customer details but publish the total and how long appeals take.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you actually leave the fraud team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When a paid utility vacancy gives me a written offer at rent-covering pay and proper training. I’m not resigning for a course advert.

Customers should see **appeal times** alongside error rates.
think: I want to leave the fraud desk **by choice**.
A decade could clear **my MBA loan** before 2036.
do: Ask the **association** to negotiate input before AI rules change.

feel: I feel **uneasy** but have room to plan.

steps.text: Ask the staff association to negotiate input before AI fraud rules change

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My thinking-heavy role could vanish before I finish a supervised trade program, and three months saved is not much for a new start. A written transition agreement and paid apprenticeship with rent-covering wages would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask what happens to the small shop after a machine freezes its account by mistake. A frozen account can close a shop before an appeal form is even read.

headlineQuote: A frozen account can close a shop before an appeal form is even read.
portrait: **Marco**, 27, leads fraud reviewers at a large payments company and has an MBA.
His typical pay and **three-month reserve** allow testing, but rent sets a firm wage floor.
He uses **AI daily** and measures wrongful freezes before changing live rules.
He pursues **paid utility training** while asking the staff association to negotiate clear terms.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his thinking-heavy role before he completes a supervised trade program.
whatWouldHelp: A written **transition agreement** and a paid apprenticeship covering rent would make the switch possible.
